title: Heavy and light, full and empty
keyIdea: Hold one thing in each hand: the heavy one pulls your hand down. On a balance scale the heavier side goes down and the lighter side goes up. Big things are not always heavy: a big balloon is lighter than a small stone. A cup is full when the water reaches the top, empty when there is none left, and half full when the water stops at the middle.

kid: Hold a book in one hand and a feather in the other. The book pulls your hand down. The book is heavy. The feather is light.
A scale is like two hands. Put a thing on each side. The heavy side goes down. The light side goes up.
Big is not the same as heavy. A big balloon is full of air, so it is light. A small stone is heavy. Feel it or use the scale to find out.
Pour water in a cup. When it reaches the top, the cup is full. Pour it all out and the cup is empty. Water up to the middle means half full.
adult: This is the start of measures in the early years. Development Matters for 3 and 4 year olds asks children to make comparisons between objects relating to size, length, weight and capacity. In Year 1 the National Curriculum names the words: mass or weight (heavy, light, heavier than, lighter than) and capacity (full, empty, more than, less than, half full). US Common Core K.MD.A.2 asks children to compare two objects and say which has more of a measurable attribute.

At this age children compare directly, with no units: hefting one object in each hand, then using a simple balance, where the heavier pan goes down. Capacity is learned through water and sand play, filling and emptying containers and using full, empty and half full. Measuring with cubes or cups comes later.

Common mistakes: believing the bigger object must be heavier (size and mass are confused), reading the balance the wrong way so that the side that rises is called heavier, calling a cup full when it is nearly full, and calling a cup empty when a little is left. Ask 'how do you know?' so the child points to the scale or the top of the cup.

In the lab your child drags things onto a balance and picks the heavier or lighter one, tests big light things against small heavy ones, pours water to full, empty and half full against a halfway line, and names how full a jar, bowl or cup is.

familyTip: At bath time give your child two cups and ask for one full and one empty, then one half full. At the shops let them hold two bags and say which is heavier, then check together with the scales.

visual.caption: Heavy or light? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the heavier and lighter thing on a balance, test big light things, and pour a cup full, empty and half full.

practice.prompt: On the scale the book side goes down and the feather side goes up. Which is heavy and which is light?
choices: The book is heavy, the feather is light
The feather is heavy, the book is light
practice.hint: The heavy side pulls the scale down.
practice.explain: The book side went down, so the book is heavy. The feather side went up, so the feather is light.

practice.prompt: The apple balances {n} blocks. The scale is level. How many blocks is the apple as heavy as?
practice.hint: Level means both sides are just as heavy.
practice.explain: The scale is level, so the apple is as heavy as the {n} blocks.

practice.prompt: Which is heavier: a big balloon or a small stone?
practice.hint: Big is not the same as heavy. Think about holding them.
practice.explain: The balloon is big but full of air. The small stone pulls your hand down more, so it is heavier.

practice.prompt: A full jug holds {n} cups of water. You pour out all {n} cups. How many cups of water are left in the jug?
practice.hint: You poured out every cup. What is left?
practice.explain: All {n} cups came out, so 0 are left. The jug is empty.

pool.prompt: Water comes right up to the top of the cup. The cup is…
pool.hint: Look at where the water stops.
pool.explain: Water right to the top means the cup is full.

pool.prompt: One side of the scale goes up. The thing on that side is…
pool.hint: Which side does the heavy thing pull?
pool.explain: The heavy thing pulls its side down, so the side that goes up has the lighter thing.

pool.prompt: A teddy balances {n} blocks on the scale. How many blocks is the teddy as heavy as?
pool.hint: When the scale is level, both sides are just as heavy.
pool.explain: The scale is level with {n} blocks, so the teddy is as heavy as {n} blocks.

pool.prompt: A cup has a little water at the bottom. Is it empty?
choices: No, there is still some water
pool.hint: Empty means no water at all. Is there any left?
pool.explain: A little water is still water, so the cup is not empty. Empty means nothing inside.

pool.prompt: Which is lighter to hold: a leaf or a pumpkin?
pool.hint: Which one would pull your hand down?
pool.explain: The pumpkin pulls your hand down. The leaf hardly does, so the leaf is lighter.

pool.prompt: The water stops at the middle of the jar. The jar is…
pool.hint: Is it at the top, at the middle, or gone?
pool.explain: Water up to the middle means half full.

pool.prompt: A big empty box and a small hammer. Which pulls the scale down?
pool.hint: Big is not the same as heavy.
pool.explain: The hammer is small but heavy. The empty box is big but light, so the hammer side goes down.

pool.prompt: The bucket is full after {n} scoops of sand. How many scoops do you pour in to make it full?
pool.hint: Full means the sand reaches the top. Count the scoops until it does.
pool.explain: It takes {n} scoops for the sand to reach the top, so {n} scoops make the bucket full.
